name: 4SRT
title: 4SRT SRT Climbing Systems & Gear
meta: 4SRT climbing gear for single rope technique: SRT systems and hardware for arborists who want to move efficiently through the canopy on a stationary rope.
intro: 4SRT is a name tree climbers run into when they start looking at single rope technique. 4SRT gear is built around SRT climbing systems that help climbers ascend and work on a stationary line.
about: Single rope technique has changed how a lot of climbers get into the tree and move around once they are up there. Ascending on a stationary rope saves energy on tall trees, and a well set up system makes the switch between ascent and work positioning cleaner. 4SRT focuses on that side of climbing.

If you are moving from moving-rope work to SRT, take the time to learn the system on the ground first, check that every component is compatible with your rope diameter, and follow the manufacturer's instructions for setup. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.
known_for: Gear for ascending a stationary rope
Components for work positioning on SRT

If you are adding Arb Climber gear to your kit, read the product's instructions and confirm it works with your rope, hitch and connectors. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.

name: Aspen
title: Aspen Alkylate 2-Stroke Fuel for Chainsaws
meta: Aspen alkylate 2-stroke fuel for chainsaws and handheld power gear. Premixed, low in harmful compounds and ready to pour, so you skip mixing on the truck.
intro: Aspen makes alkylate petrol, and Aspen 2 stroke fuel is the premixed version a lot of saw users keep for their chainsaws, pole saws and blowers. It comes ready to use, so there is no mixing on the tailgate.
about: Alkylate fuel is a cleaner-burning petrol with far fewer of the aromatic compounds found in regular pump gas. For anyone running a saw all day, that means less of the exhaust you breathe while you buck and limb. Aspen 2 is premixed with two-stroke oil, while Aspen 4 is the version for four-stroke equipment.

Many operators also like alkylate for storage. It does not contain ethanol, so it holds up better in saws that sit between jobs and in seasonal equipment. Check your saw manufacturer's guidance on fuel and mix ratio, and when you switch fuels, let the saw run and confirm it is tuned properly before putting it back to work.

name: At Height
title: At Height Work-at-Height Gear for Tree Care
meta: At Height gear for work at height. What tree crews should know before adding fall protection and climbing equipment to their kit, and how to keep it in service.
intro: At Height is a brand name associated with gear for working off the ground. For tree crews, any at-height equipment should be chosen for the task and inspected before use.
about: Tree work mixes climbing, aerial lifts and ladders, and each of those calls for the right fall protection and positioning gear. Before you buy, be clear about whether a piece is meant for climbing in the tree, bucket work or general fall arrest, since the standards and use cases differ.

Keep records of when gear went into service, store it out of the sun and away from fuel and chemicals, and retire it after a fall or when inspection turns up damage. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.
known_for: Gear for climbers and aerial crews

name: Beaver State Plastics
title: Beaver State Plastics for Tree & Saw Work
meta: Beaver State Plastics products for tree and saw work. A plain look at the brand and what to check before plastic gear goes into your truck or saw kit.
intro: Beaver State Plastics is a name some tree and forestry workers know from plastic gear for the job. Plastic tools and accessories earn their place when they are tough, light and easy to replace.
about: A lot of the small gear that rides in a saw kit is plastic for good reason: it is light, it will not wreck a chain if you touch it with the saw, and it is cheap enough to replace when it cracks. That is the general category Beaver State Plastics fits into.
Check plastic gear for cracks, mushroomed heads and brittleness, especially after a cold season or long sun exposure, and replace it rather than nursing it through another day.
known_for: Plastic gear for tree and forestry work

name: BigFoot
title: BigFoot Outrigger Pads for Bucket Trucks & Cranes
meta: BigFoot outrigger pads spread the load under bucket trucks, cranes and lifts so outriggers do not sink into lawns, soft soil or damage driveways on tree jobs.
intro: BigFoot makes outrigger pads that sit under the feet of bucket trucks, cranes and other equipment with stabilizers. BigFoot outrigger pads spread the load so the machine stays level and the customer's yard stays intact.
about: Setting up an aerial lift or crane on a residential job means dealing with soft turf, irrigation lines and pavers. An outrigger pad gives the stabilizer foot a bigger footprint, which reduces ground pressure and helps keep the machine stable through the lift. It also protects driveways and lawns from punch-through and gouges.

Size the pad to the outrigger load and the ground conditions, not just to what fits in the truck. Follow the equipment manufacturer's setup requirements, place pads on firm, level ground where you can, and inspect them for cracks or deformation before each use.

name: Boss
title: Boss Gear for Tree Crews
meta: Boss gear for tree crews. A practical look at the brand and what to check before you buy, so the gear you add to your truck holds up to real tree work.
intro: Boss is a brand name that turns up in tree care gear lists. As with anything going on the truck, Boss gear should be matched to the job and checked before use.
about: Tree crews go through gear fast. Gloves wear through, tools get dropped from height and anything left on the trailer takes weather all season. Before you buy, look at how the product is built, what it is meant for and how easy it is to replace.
If a Boss product is used for anything safety related, read the manufacturer's information and confirm it suits the task. Retire worn or damaged gear rather than pushing it through one more job.

name: Gap Arborist Supply
title: Gap Arborist Supply House Essentials
meta: Gap Arborist Supply house essentials: slings, rope snaps, chafe sleeves, chipper knives and cabling hardware, the everyday basics every tree crew goes through.
intro: Gap Arborist Supply is our house label for the everyday essentials tree crews go through: slings, rope snaps, chafe sleeves, chipper knives and cabling hardware. These are the plain, generic basics that keep a job moving.
about: Not every piece of gear needs a big brand name. A chafe sleeve that protects a rope from bark, a steel snap for a lanyard or a set of chipper knives is a working part, and what matters is that it is the right size and the right type for your setup. The Gap Arborist Supply label groups those generic items together so they are easy to find.

We list the basics we would want on our own trucks and describe them plainly. Always check the item against your equipment before ordering, such as chipper model and knife dimensions or rope diameter and sleeve size. Anything used for life support or rigging must be rated for the load, meet the applicable standard, and be inspected before use.

name: Land
title: Land Helmets & Earmuffs for Tree Work
meta: Land helmets and earmuffs for tree work. Head and hearing protection for climbers and ground crews running saws and chippers, plus tips on fit and care.
intro: Land makes helmets and earmuffs used by people who work around saws and trees. Land helmets and hearing protection are part of the basic PPE every climber and ground worker should wear.
about: Head protection on a tree job covers falling wood, dropped tools and bumps while climbing. Hearing protection covers the steady noise of saws, chippers and grinders. Land offers both, and a helmet with matched earmuffs means you are not fighting gear that does not fit together.

Pick a helmet that meets the standard your work requires, adjust it so it stays put when you look up, and replace it after a hard impact or when the shell or suspension shows damage. Replace earmuff cushions when they stiffen or crack so the seal holds.
known_for: Hearing protection for saw and chipper noise

about: Arborist gear works as a system. A piece that is great on its own can still cause trouble if it does not suit your rope, connectors or the way you work. Read the product information, test it on the ground and get comfortable with it before relying on it in the tree.

Where any PaulHaul product is part of a climbing or rigging system, use it within its rated limits. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.

name: Preformed Line Products
title: Preformed Line Products Cable Grips & Dead-Ends
meta: Preformed Line Products cable grips and dead-ends for tree cabling and guying. Helical grips terminate strand cleanly so systems install fast and stay put.
intro: Preformed Line Products makes helical cable grips and dead-ends used to terminate strand. In tree care, Preformed Line Products dead-ends are a common way to finish the ends of steel cable in support and guying systems.
about: A preformed dead-end wraps around the cable and grips it along its length, which gives a clean termination without clamps. For arborists installing steel cabling in trees, or guying newly planted or leaning trees, that means quicker installs and fewer loose parts.

Grips are sized to a specific strand diameter and type, so match them exactly to your cable. Install them per the manufacturer's directions and the applicable best management practices for tree support systems, and do not reuse grips beyond what the manufacturer allows.

name: Razor-Back
title: Razor-Back Tools: Shovels, Axes & Striking Tools
meta: Razor-Back tools for ground crews: shovels, axes and striking tools built for digging, root work and cleanup. A look at where they fit on tree jobs.
intro: Razor-Back makes heavy-duty hand tools like shovels, axes and other striking and digging tools. Razor-Back tools are the kind ground crews keep in the truck for stump cleanup, root work and site work.
about: A lot of tree work happens at ground level: digging out around a stump, cutting roots, cleaning up chips and backfilling. A solid shovel and a reliable axe are part of the kit, and Razor-Back is a familiar name in that category.

Keep edges sharp, check handles for cracks or loose heads before each use, and wear eye protection and gloves when chopping roots or swinging a striking tool. Replace a damaged handle rather than taping it.

name: Rigguy
title: Rigguy Tree Cabling & Guying Hardware
meta: Rigguy cabling hardware for tree support and guying systems. What arborists should know about matching hardware to cable and installing support systems.
intro: Rigguy makes cabling and guying hardware. For arborists, Rigguy hardware is part of the toolkit for installing tree support systems and guying trees.
about: Cabling a tree is about adding support to weak unions and heavy limbs without stopping the tree from moving naturally. That takes the right cable, terminations and anchors, all sized to work together. Rigguy hardware fits into that category.

Match every component to the cable size and type you are installing, follow the manufacturer's directions, and follow current best management practices for tree support systems. Inspect installed systems on a regular schedule.

name: The Splice Shop
title: The Splice Shop Spliced Rope, Slings & Lanyards
meta: The Splice Shop makes spliced rope products for tree work: eye-spliced lines, slings and lanyards. What to know about ordering spliced rope for your system.
intro: The Splice Shop makes spliced rope products. Arborists know The Splice Shop for eye-spliced lines, slings and lanyards built to order.
about: A sewn or spliced eye makes a rope easier to rig and cleaner to run through hardware than a knot, and it keeps more of the rope's strength. Spliced slings and lanyards are a staple for both climbing and rigging, and a shop that splices is the place to get them.

When ordering, give the rope type, diameter, length and eye size, and confirm the splice is right for how you will use it. Inspect splices for slipping, cut strands or worn covers. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.

name: R-Easy Climbing
title: R-Easy Climbing Fox Harness & Climbing Gear
meta: R-Easy Climbing makes climbing gear including the Fox harness. A look at the brand, what to check in a climbing harness and how to keep it in service.
intro: R-Easy Climbing is a climbing gear brand known for the Fox harness. If you are looking at the R-Easy Climbing Fox harness, check fit and intended use before it becomes your daily saddle.
about: A harness or saddle is the piece of gear you live in all day, so fit matters as much as features. Look at leg loop comfort, how the bridge sets up, where your attachment points sit and how much room there is for saws and hardware.

Read the manufacturer's information on intended use, confirm the attachment points work with your connectors, and retire the harness when webbing, stitching or buckles show damage. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.

Practice with new gear close to the ground before you take it up. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.

name: Reecoil

intro: Reecoil is a brand name that shows up in tree care gear lists. Before adding Reecoil gear to your kit, check what it is designed for and how it fits the way you work.

If a Reecoil product is part of a climbing or rigging system, use it within its rated limits. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.

name: Atlas

intro: Atlas is a brand name tree crews may see in gear lists. Like any working gear, Atlas products should be chosen for the job and replaced when they wear out.
about: Tree work is hard on equipment. What lasts is gear that fits the task, is easy to keep clean and does not get in the way when you are climbing, rigging or feeding the chipper.
Read the product details before you buy, and if an Atlas item is used for protection or safety, make sure it is rated for the hazard you face and retire it when it is damaged.

about: Tree crews pick up gear from all kinds of sources, from big manufacturers to smaller outfits. What matters is the same either way: the item has to suit the task, be built well enough for daily use and come with clear information on its limits.
Anything used for climbing or rigging must be rated for the load, meet the applicable standard and be inspected before use. Retire damaged gear rather than nursing it along.

If an Edge product is protective equipment, make sure it is rated for the hazard you face. If it is used for climbing or rigging, it must meet the applicable standard and be inspected before use.

name: ERB Safety
title: ERB Safety Glasses & PPE for Tree Work
meta: ERB Safety glasses and PPE for tree crews. Eye protection and safety gear for saw work, chipping and brush cleanup, plus tips on fit, lenses and care.
intro: ERB Safety makes safety eyewear and other personal protective equipment. ERB Safety glasses are a practical choice for ground crews and climbers who need eye protection on every cut.
about: Sawdust, chips, bark and twigs are constant eye hazards on a tree job, and the chipper throws debris at the person feeding it. Safety glasses are cheap insurance, and having a few spare pairs on the truck means nobody works without them.

Pick lenses for the light you work in, clear for shade and overcast days and tinted for bright sun, and look for a fit that stays put under a helmet and with earmuffs. Choose eyewear marked to the safety standard your work requires and replace scratched lenses that cut your vision.
known_for: Eye protection for saw and chipper work

name: Gibbs
title: Gibbs Ascenders for Rope Climbing
meta: Gibbs ascenders for rope climbing. A look at the Gibbs cam ascender, where it fits in SRT and foot-ascent setups, and how to inspect it before every climb.
intro: Gibbs makes rope ascenders used by tree climbers, cavers and rope workers. The Gibbs ascender uses a cam that grips the rope, and climbers often use it as a foot ascender or as part of an SRT system.
about: Gibbs ascenders have been around for a long time and are known for a simple, rugged cam design. Arborists who climb on a stationary rope use them to make ascending more efficient, often paired with another ascender or a hitch system.

Confirm the ascender is compatible with your rope diameter and sheath, and learn how to rig and release it correctly before you leave the ground. Check the cam, spring and pins for wear and grit. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.

name: Hobbs
title: Hobbs Lowering Device for Tree Rigging
meta: The Hobbs lowering device is a friction device for tree rigging. Learn how it helps ground crews control loads when lowering wood and what to check first.
intro: Hobbs makes lowering devices for tree rigging. The Hobbs lowering device gives the ground crew controlled friction on the rigging line so pieces can be let down smoothly instead of crashing to the ground.
about: Lowering wood safely is all about friction control. A lowering device anchored at the base of the tree lets the groundworker add or take away wraps to match the load, then let the piece run or hold it. The Hobbs is one of the established devices in that role.

Size your rigging line, slings and hardware to the loads you will see, set the device up per the manufacturer's instructions, and keep hands clear of the rope where it enters the device. Rigging forces climb fast with shock loading, so plan cuts that keep loads under control. Rigging should only be done by trained crews.

name: International Society of Arboriculture
title: ISA Arborist Study Guides & Publications
meta: International Society of Arboriculture publications for arborists: certification study guides, best management practices and references for tree care pros.
intro: The International Society of Arboriculture (ISA) publishes study guides and references for the tree care profession. The ISA arborist study guide and best management practices are standard reading for anyone working toward certification.
about: ISA runs the ISA Certified Arborist program and publishes the material many people use to prepare for it. Beyond exam prep, ISA's best management practices series covers topics such as pruning, tree support systems and tree risk assessment, and is a common reference on the job.

If you are studying for an exam, check which edition of a guide your test is based on. For daily work, keep the relevant best management practices on hand alongside the ANSI A300 standards and ANSI Z133 safety requirements that apply to your work.

name: No-Spill
title: No-Spill Gas Cans for Saws & Power Equipment
meta: No-Spill gas cans for chainsaws and power equipment. Push-button pouring that cuts down on spilled fuel when you refuel saws, blowers and chippers.
intro: No-Spill makes fuel cans with a push-button spout designed to control the pour. A No-Spill gas can makes refueling chainsaws and handheld gear cleaner and less wasteful.
about: Refueling saws on a tree job happens often and usually in a hurry. A can that lets you control the flow and shut it off quickly means less fuel on the saw, the ground and your hands, and less fire risk around hot equipment.

Use a can approved for the fuel you carry, keep caps closed when stored, and secure cans upright in the truck. Refuel with the engine off and cool, away from sparks, and wipe up spills before restarting.

name: Phoenix
title: Phoenix Gear for Tree Crews

Anything used for climbing or rigging must be rated for the load. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.

name: Ropetek
title: Ropetek Rigging Gear for Arborists
meta: Ropetek rigging gear for arborists: equipment for lowering and moving wood. What to know about matching rigging gear to loads and keeping crews safe.
intro: Ropetek makes rigging gear used by tree crews. Ropetek equipment fits into the rigging side of the job, where controlled lowering and good friction management matter most.
about: Rigging takes a team: the climber setting up the cut, the groundworker managing the line and the gear in between. Rigging equipment such as lowering devices, blocks and related hardware has to be sized for the forces involved, which can be far higher than the weight of the piece when a load is shock-loaded.

Check the rated limits of each Ropetek product, match it to your rope and slings, and follow the manufacturer's instructions for setup. Inspect rigging gear before each job and retire anything damaged. Rigging should only be done by trained crews.

name: Singing Tree
title: Singing Tree Rope Runner & Climbing Hardware
meta: Singing Tree climbing hardware for arborists, including the Rope Runner mechanical friction device. What to know before it goes in your climbing system.
intro: Singing Tree makes climbing hardware for arborists, and the Singing Tree Rope Runner is its best-known piece: a mechanical device climbers use in place of a friction hitch.
about: Mechanical devices have become a common choice for climbers who want consistent friction and easy tending on both moving and stationary rope systems. The Rope Runner is one of the devices that helped make that shift, and Singing Tree also makes related hardware for climbing setups.

Confirm your rope is on the device manufacturer's list of compatible ropes, set it up exactly as the instructions show, and practice near the ground before working at height. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.
known_for: Mechanical friction for SRT and MRS

name: Tylaska
title: Tylaska Low-Friction Rings & Rigging Hardware
meta: Tylaska low-friction rings and rigging hardware. Marine-grade hardware arborists use to redirect rope and build cleaner climbing and rigging setups.
intro: Tylaska makes precision rigging hardware, best known for low-friction rings and marine snap shackles. Arborists use Tylaska low-friction rings to redirect rope and reduce wear in rigging and climbing setups.
about: Tylaska's background is high-performance sailing hardware, where light weight and smooth rope running matter. That same hardware has found a place in tree work, especially low-friction rings used as redirects, in false crotch setups and in some climbing and rigging systems.

A low-friction ring is not a pulley, so expect more friction and heat than a sheave would give, and size it to the rope diameter and loads you plan for. Check the rating for your use, inspect for grooves or burrs, and follow the manufacturer's information. Any gear that holds a person must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before each use, and be used by trained climbers.

name: WD-40
title: WD-40 for Saws, Tools & Equipment Care
meta: WD-40 for tree crew tool care: loosen stuck bolts, displace moisture, clean sap and protect saws, hand tools and trailer gear from rust between jobs.
intro: WD-40 is the familiar multi-use spray found in nearly every truck and shop. For tree crews, WD-40 helps loosen stuck fasteners, push out moisture and clean sap and grime off tools.
about: Saws, pruners, wedges and trailer hitches all take a beating from weather and sap. A quick spray and wipe helps keep rust off bare steel, frees up seized nuts and makes cleanup easier at the end of the day.

Keep it off climbing and rigging soft goods and away from ropes, harnesses and friction hitches, and do not use it on any life-support hardware unless the manufacturer says it is acceptable. Wipe excess off handles so they do not get slick.

name: Wonder Grip
title: Wonder Grip Gloves for Tree Work
meta: Wonder Grip gloves for tree crews. Coated work gloves with good grip and feel for climbing, rigging, handling brush and feeding the chipper safely.
intro: Wonder Grip makes coated work gloves known for grip and dexterity. Wonder Grip gloves are a common pick for climbers and ground crews who want feel and grip without bulk.
about: Gloves on a tree job need to do a lot: protect against bark, splinters and rope burn, keep grip on wet wood and still let you tie knots and clip carabiners. Coated gloves in the Wonder Grip style are popular because they are thin enough for dexterity and grippy enough for handling rope and limbs.

Keep a few pairs on the truck, since coated gloves wear out on rope and brush. Do not rely on general work gloves for chainsaw cut protection, and be careful wearing loose gloves when feeding a chipper.
known_for: Grip for rope and brush handling
